citation: Kononowicz, A. A., Woodham, L. A., Edelbring, S., Stathakarou, N., Davies, D., Saxena, N., Tudor Car, L., Carlstedt-Duke, J., Car, J., & Zary, N. (2019). Virtual patient simulations in health professions education: Systematic review and meta-analysis by the Digital Health Education Collaboration. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 21(7), e14676. https://doi.org/10.2196/14676
discipline: health professions education (systematic review & meta-analysis, Digital Health Education Collaboration series)
thesis: A Cochrane-methodology systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 51 RCTs/cRCTs (N=4,696) evaluating screen-based virtual patient (VP) simulations in health professions education across four comparisons (VP vs traditional education, VP-blended vs traditional education, VP vs other digital education, VP design-variant comparisons); VP matches traditional education on knowledge (SMD=0.11, ns) but shows moderate-large gains for skills (SMD=0.90); design-variant (sim-vs-sim) comparisons are mostly non-significant for knowledge and mixed for skills; the review explicitly joins Friedman and Cook's call to abandon media-comparative research in favor of theory-grounded, adequately powered design-variant studies.

sections.title: Background & Introduction
sections.summary: Defines virtual patients as interactive digital simulations of clinical scenarios (screen-based, not 3D-immersive), situates them within Kolb's experiential learning theory, and notes prior narrative reviews plus two earlier systematic reviews/meta-analyses (Cook, Erwin & Triola 2010; Consorti et al. 2012) that this study updates. Explicitly excludes 3D virtual learning environments as out of scope, reserving them for a sibling DHEC review (ref 13).

sections.title: Methods (Eligibility, Search, Analysis)
sections.summary: Cochrane methodology + random-effects meta-analysis; 7 databases searched 1990-Sept 2018; RCTs/cRCTs only, crossover trials excluded. A priori excludes 2-arm comparisons against a no-intervention control group (an earlier VP-specific meta-analysis already showed a large effect there) -- the review targets virtual-patient-vs-traditional-education, blended, vs-other-digital-education, and design-variant comparisons only.

sections.title: Results -- Knowledge, Skills, Attitudes, Satisfaction, Secondary Outcomes
sections.summary: 51 trials, 4,696 participants, from 44,054 screened citations. Knowledge: SMD=0.11 (95% CI -0.17 to 0.39, I2=74%, n=927), no significant difference vs traditional education. Skills: SMD=0.90 (95% CI 0.49-1.32, I2=88%, n=897), moderate-to-large advantage for virtual patients (clinical reasoning, procedural, team skills). Blended VP+traditional vs traditional: knowledge SMD=0.73, skills SMD=0.60. Design-variant (sim-vs-sim) comparisons: of 8 knowledge studies only Friedman et al. found a significant difference (pedagogic/guided > problem-solving/high-fidelity, P<.01); the rest (linear/branched, scaffolded/nonscaffolded, worked/unworked, usability extensions, self-determined/mandatory, spaced/nonspaced, solving/constructing) showed no significant differences. Skills design-variant comparisons (4 studies) were more mixed: feedback type, narrative-vs-problem-solving, and scaffolding significant; solving-vs-constructing not. Attitudes/satisfaction mostly measured via item-by-item surveys with inconsistent results; self-efficacy and confidence sometimes lower in virtual-patient groups despite equal/better objective performance. Post hoc active/passive control split (via albatross plots) explained heterogeneity better than any pre-registered subgroup: VP shows large effects vs passive controls (lecture, reading), small/negative vs active controls (group discussion, mannequin).

sections.title: Discussion & Outlook
sections.summary: Interprets the knowledge/skills split via Bloom's taxonomy -- little added value at lower cognitive levels, larger benefit where knowledge is applied in problem-solving. Explicitly joins Friedman and Cook's call to abandon media-comparative research (comparing formats like paper vs digital) as uninterpretable given confounds, urging future work toward design-variant, theory-grounded, adequately powered studies instead.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.summary: Low-to-modest, mixed-quality evidence: virtual patients are at least as effective as traditional education for knowledge and more effective for skills, particularly clinical reasoning. Recommends further research into design variants rather than further media comparison.

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: Knowledge outcome; pooled SMD=0.11 (95% CI -0.17 to 0.39, I2=74%, n=927) vs traditional education; no significant difference.

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: Skills outcome; pooled SMD=0.90 (95% CI 0.49-1.32, I2=88%, n=897) vs traditional education; moderate-to-large advantage, concentrated in clinical reasoning, procedural, and team skills.

constructs.label: self-efficacy
constructs.treatment: Treated within 'attitudes' (confidence, preparedness, comfort, perceived ability); mixed evidence; some studies show self-reported confidence lower in VP groups despite equal/better objective performance.

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: Treated within 'satisfaction,' specifically its 'comfort in use' sub-dimension (engagement/motivation, positive climate, enjoyment); most item-by-item comparisons indifferent rather than favorable.

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: Treated obliquely via design-variant studies: Friedman et al.'s guided/pedagogic VP format beat a high-fidelity/unguided format on knowledge and satisfaction; Dankbaar et al. separately hypothesize high fidelity raises motivation but distracts novices.

conditions.label: screen-based virtual patient / sim
conditions.design: 51 RCTs/cRCTs, N=4,696 (from 44,054 screened citations), across 4 comparison arms: VP-vs-traditional (25 studies), VP-blended-vs-traditional (11), VP-vs-other-digital (5), VP design-variant (10). Deliberately excludes 3D-immersive VP variants (deferred to a companion DHEC VR review) and VP-vs-no-intervention comparisons (settled by an earlier VP-specific meta-analysis).

conditions.label: conventional instruction (control)
conditions.design: Traditional-education controls: reading assignment (6 studies), lecture (4), group assignment (4), mannequin-based training (4), standardized patients (1), ward-based (1), mixed forms (5). Post hoc active/passive split (via albatross plots) found VP large vs passive controls, small/negative vs active controls -- explained heterogeneity better than any of 15 pre-registered subgroup analyses.

conditions.label: review / meta-analytic aggregate
conditions.design: Cochrane-methodology systematic review + random-effects meta-analysis (Review Manager 5.3); I2 heterogeneity; GRADE quality-of-evidence downgrading; Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment across 7 domains; overall verdict low-to-modest, mixed-quality evidence.

readings.claim: Virtual patients are as effective as traditional education for knowledge outcomes (SMD=0.11, ns) but more effective for skills outcomes (SMD=0.90, moderate-large).

VP's advantage over traditional education is contingent on the comparator: large vs passive controls (lecture, reading), small or negative vs active controls (group discussion, mannequin-based training).

Design-variant (sim-vs-sim) comparisons are mostly non-significant for knowledge (7 of 8 studies) and more mixed for skills (3 of 4 studies significant, each via a specific mechanism -- feedback, narrative structure, scaffolding -- rather than a generic effect).

Media-comparative research (VP vs traditional format) should be abandoned as uninterpretable given uncontrolled confounds; future research should focus on theory-grounded, adequately powered design-variant studies.

Self-reported confidence is sometimes lower in VP groups despite equal/better objective performance, tentatively attributed to disbelief in computer-based methods or anxiety about reduced direct-patient contact.
Guided/pedagogic VP design outperformed high-fidelity/unguided VP design on knowledge and satisfaction, a counter-intuitive result against a naive 'more fidelity is better' prior.

concepts.term: active vs passive control split (albatross plot)

interlocutors.name: Cook, David A. (Cook, Erwin & Triola 2010 VP-specific meta-analysis, ref [38])
interlocutors.role: prior meta-analysis this review extends; distinct from the technology-enhanced-simulation meta-analysis at ped-sec-15

interlocutors.name: Cook, David A. (media-comparative-research critique, ref [104])
interlocutors.role: co-source, with Friedman, of the critique that media-comparative research is uninterpretable; this review joins the call to abandon it

interlocutors.name: Consorti (2012 meta-analysis, ref [39])
interlocutors.role: second prior meta-analysis this review updates

interlocutors.name: Friedman, Charles P. (media-comparative-research critique, ref [103]; also primary author of the significant design-variant study, ref [96])
interlocutors.role: source of the media-comparative-research critique and of the review's single significant knowledge-domain design-variant finding

interlocutors.name: Kolb, David A.
interlocutors.role: experiential learning theory grounding the pedagogy of virtual patients

interlocutors.name: Bloom, Benjamin
interlocutors.role: taxonomy cited for interpreting the knowledge/skills split

tensions.axis: media-comparative research (VP vs traditional format) vs design-variant research (VP internal-feature comparison)
tensions.note: The review's own structural pivot: it reports media-comparative results (its largest evidence base) while explicitly arguing, in its Outlook, that this comparison type should be abandoned in favor of the much smaller design-variant literature it also reports.

tensions.axis: VP's advantage over traditional education is large vs passive controls but negligible vs active controls
tensions.note: Complicates a simple 'VP beats traditional education' headline; the effect is contingent on what traditional education is doing (passive transmission vs active engagement), not on VP alone.

tensions.axis: objective performance gains vs self-reported confidence
tensions.note: Some studies show VP groups performing equal or better on objective measures while reporting lower confidence than traditional-education groups -- an affect/performance dissociation not resolved by this review.
